title: Space Telescope Finds Clues of Giant Crashes Near Young Stars
summary:
Long ago, the young Earth crashed into a Mars-sized object called Theia. Scientists think pieces from that crash came together to form our Moon.

Now, NASA's James Webb Space Telescope is helping scientists look for similar crashes around young stars. A team led by Kate Su studied 21 rare disks of warm dust close to young stars. Only about 1% of young stars show this kind of dust.

The scientists studied the minerals in the dust. About one-third of the disks have lots of silica, a material found in a volcanic glass called obsidian. The team thinks these came from very powerful crashes between Mars-sized worlds. The other disks seem to come from gentler bumps, including between Moon-sized objects.

"This is the first time we have gathered enough systems to truly understand this subclass that we call extreme debris disks," Su said. The study was published on October 1.
why_it_matters: Learning about crashes around other stars helps us understand how our own Earth and Moon were made.

Space telescopes like Webb help scientists see the dust left over from these crashes.
Article_Structure: WHO: A team of scientists led by Kate Su, using NASA's James Webb Space Telescope
WHAT: They found signs of giant crashes between big worlds in dusty disks
WHERE: Around young stars far out in space
WHY: To learn how planets like Earth, and our Moon, may have formed
